title: Index Selection, Selectivity, Sequential Scans, and When Indexes Hurt
description: Index Selection, Selectivity, Sequential Scans, and When Indexes Hurt. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Explain selectivity and its effect on access-path cost.
Explain why PostgreSQL may choose sequential scan despite an index.
Compare index, bitmap heap, and sequential scans.
Identify index write, storage, cache, vacuum, and operational costs.
Use workload evidence to justify adding or removing indexes.

mentalModel.text: An index is an option, not an instruction. If a query needs five rows from a million, an index can save a lot of work. If it needs half the table, finding rows through an index and then jumping around the table may cost more than reading the table in order. PostgreSQL estimates those costs and chooses the path it expects to be cheapest.

blocks.text: Selectivity tells you how much of the table matches a condition. Searching for one rare email is highly selective; searching for a status shared by most orders is not. Cardinality is the actual or estimated number of matching rows.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='shipped';

blocks.title: Three terms for judging an index
rows: How small a share of rows matches a condition.
One rare email is highly selective; a status held by 70% of orders is not.
How many rows match, estimated by the planner or observed in execution.
The planner expects 100 rows but the query actually returns 40,000.
The method used to find those rows.
An index scan can help for a few rows; a sequential scan can win for a broad result.

blocks.text: A sequential scan reads table pages in order and checks each row. An index scan finds matching keys and then fetches their table rows, which can involve many scattered reads. A bitmap heap scan collects row locations by page to reduce random visits, but usually cannot preserve the index's ordering.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id,total_amount FROM orders WHERE status='shipped';

steps.title: Identify query shape
steps.description: Write down predicates, joins, ordering, limit, and selected columns.

steps.title: Predict the mechanism
steps.description: Explain which pages, entries, or operators the database is likely to visit.

steps.title: Validate the plan
steps.description: Use actual rows and buffers to compare prediction with observed work.

blocks.text: A sequential scan can be the right choice for a small table or a query that needs many rows. Following an index and then fetching most rows one by one may cost more than reading the table pages together. An index existing does not mean PostgreSQL should use it.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled';

blocks.problem: A query filters orders with status = 'paid'. An index on status exists, but about 70% of rows match.
reasoning: Because most rows match, an index scan may fetch a large share of the table through many separate page visits.
A sequential scan can read table pages in order and be cheaper for this broad result.
Compare estimated and actual row counts, buffers, and execution time; also consider the extra write work caused by maintaining the index.
blocks.outcome: PostgreSQL does not have to use every index. For broad results, reading the table in order can be cheaper than following the index.

blocks.text: Every index must be updated when relevant rows change. Indexes use disk and memory, add work to writes and WAL, and need maintenance as rows are deleted or updated. Keeping unused indexes can slow the whole workload, not just take up space.

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.text: Before adding or dropping an index, look at real query frequency, latency, plans, write rate, and index size over a representative period. Change one thing at a time and check whether the improvement to reads is worth the extra write and storage cost.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 1
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: More indexes is not automatically better: an index may speed one query while slowing writes and consuming cache.

revisionSheet.text: Selectivity and estimated row count influence path costs.
Sequential scans can be best for small tables or broad predicates.
Bitmap heap scans group heap access but generally do not preserve index order.
Every index adds storage, write, WAL, cache, and maintenance cost.
Use representative plans and workload evidence before adding or dropping an index.

options.text: A predicate matches a small fraction of rows
A predicate matches almost every row

questions.explanation: A selective predicate narrows results substantially.

questions.prompt: Why can sequential scan beat index scan when most rows match?

options.text: Sequential page reads can beat many scattered heap fetches
PostgreSQL never uses indexes on large tables

questions.explanation: Broad results can make index navigation plus heap access more costly.

questions.prompt: What does a bitmap heap scan do?

options.text: Collects tuple locations and groups heap visits by page

questions.explanation: Bitmap scans can reduce random visits but generally do not preserve order.

questions.prompt: Why is there no universal selectivity threshold for index use?

options.text: Cost depends on size, row width, cache, correlation, estimates, and query shape

questions.explanation: The crossover depends on workload and physical costs.

questions.prompt: What is a common cost of another index on a write-heavy table?

options.text: More index maintenance, storage, and cache use
All reads become slower by definition
The table loses its primary key

questions.explanation: Indexes trade read benefit for write, storage, and maintenance cost.

questions.prompt: Safest way to investigate an unused index?

options.text: Read actual plan and buffers, compare estimates, verify query shape

questions.explanation: Plan evidence distinguishes rational sequential scans from design/estimate issues.

questions.prompt: Why can a low-cardinality status index be unhelpful for a broad predicate?

options.text: Many rows may match and require many heap visits
Low cardinality means no index entries

questions.explanation: Broad results may make a table scan cheaper.

questions.prompt: Why not drop an index based only on idx_scan?

options.text: Stats may reset and rare critical queries or constraints may rely on it

questions.explanation: Use a representative observation window and account for constraints and rare paths.

questions.prompt: Which can make sequential scan rational?

options.text: Index path requires scattered heap fetches
An index exists, therefore it must be used

questions.explanation: The planner chooses by cost; index existence alone is not decisive.

questions.prompt: What to consider before dropping a low-usage index?

options.text: Stats reset window and workload seasonality
Only idx_scan from the last minute

questions.explanation: Usage counters need context and must be balanced against cost and importance.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL is always wrong when it chooses a sequential scan while an index exists.
questions.explanation: Sequential scans can be cheaper for small tables or broad predicates.

questions.prompt: Every additional index has zero write cost if it speeds reads.
questions.explanation: Indexes add write maintenance, storage, cache, WAL, and operational cost.

interviewScenarios.prompt: An interviewer says: “The table has an index, but PostgreSQL uses a sequential scan. The planner is broken.” Respond.
strongAnswerPoints: Explain broad-result and random heap-fetch trade-offs.
Compare estimates to actual rows and inspect buffers.
Check size, row width, correlation, cache, and query shape.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Index presence does not make an index path cheapest. For broad predicates, sequential reads can beat scattered heap visits. Capture EXPLAIN ANALYZE with buffers, compare estimates with actuals, and inspect distribution and query shape before concluding the planner is wrong.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A write-heavy table has 40 indexes and disk usage is high. How rationalize the set?
strongAnswerPoints: Map indexes to queries and constraints.
Review sizes, usage over a representative window, plans, and overlapping prefixes.
Test reversible changes and monitor reads, writes, WAL, vacuum, and latency.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Map each index to queries and constraints, then balance read benefit against storage, cache, write amplification, WAL, and maintenance. Counters alone are insufficient. Test changes in stages and monitor read SLOs and write behavior.
